answer.evidence: This is a manual read of the weights, so a subtle shortcut cannot be fully ruled out. The clearly trained structure sits in the centre of the image. Hidden units 3, 8, 21, 24, 27 and 28 have coherent blocks of large positive weights over roughly rows 4-19, cols 5-18, with the largest values in the tensor (93-99, beyond the ~80 init range) concentrated there. These are nodule-brightness and nodule-extent detectors. Several units are mirror images of these: units 5, 18 and 29 have strongly negative central weights, and units 18 and 2 have negative centres with positive surrounds, i.e. centre-versus-surround or margin features. Ignoring the ReLUs, unit 3 (broad central positive weights) has a net downstream effect of about +15k integer-units toward malignant, and unit 8 about +8k. I scanned all four corners, the edge rows and columns, and the band at the top for a small, tight cluster of same-sign large weights repeated across units, which is how a marker or patch would show up. None qualified. The top-right and top rows (0-3) of units 2, 14, 16, 18, 19, 25, 29 and 30 are mildly positive-heavy (about 10-12 of 16 values positive), but the magnitudes stay within the init range. Those units also feed the output in opposite directions: units 30 and 18 push toward malignant, units 25, 19 and 2 toward benign. That pattern is not consistent with a single spurious cue. No off-nodule patch has weights clearly exceeding the random-init scale or routing consistently to one class.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly responds to bright, dense tissue in the central region where the nodule sits: larger, brighter central blobs drive malignant-leaning units such as 3 and 8. It also uses some centre-versus-surround contrast units such as 2 and 18 that encode the nodule margin and the surrounding lung.
